title: How models are trained
blurb: Where a model’s knowledge comes from — and why it stops at a date.

slides.title: Step one: read an enormous amount of text
body: A model starts out knowing nothing. It’s shown a huge amount of text — books, websites, code — and asked, over and over, to predict the next token.
Each time it guesses wrong, its internal numbers (called parameters) are nudged slightly so the right answer scores higher next time. Over time, those nudges add up to a model of how language works.

visual.caption: One training step, repeated an enormous number of times.

items.label: Adjust
items.text: The real word was “mat”, so nudge the parameters to make “mat” more likely next time.

slides.title: Step two: learning to be an assistant
body: A model fresh from step one just continues text. Ask it a question and it might carry on with more questions, as if it were writing a quiz.
So it gets further training on example conversations and on people’s ratings of its answers. This teaches it to follow instructions, be helpful and decline harmful requests.

visual.caption: Example replies written for illustration.
visual.question: What is the capital of France?

cards.label: Before assistant training
cards.text: What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Spain?

cards.label: After assistant training
cards.text: The capital of France is Paris.

slides.title: Why it has a knowledge cut-off
body: Training text is collected up to a certain date. Once training ends, what the model has learned is fixed — it doesn’t keep reading the news.
That’s why a model may not know about recent events, and why some apps add web search: it puts fresh information into the context window.

visual.caption: The model’s knowledge and the app around it are different things.

items.heading: Fixed after training
items.text: Nothing after the cut-off date is in the model itself.

items.heading: Doesn’t learn as you chat
items.text: Your conversation doesn’t change the model’s parameters.

items.heading: Fresh facts come via context
items.text: Search results or pasted documents can fill the gap for one request.

slides.title: Patterns, not a database
body: A model doesn’t keep a copy of everything it read. What it learned is spread across its parameters as patterns.
That makes it good at things it saw a lot of, and shakier on details it saw rarely.

visual.caption: This is why the same model can be brilliant on one question and wrong on the next.

items.heading: Strong on the common
items.text: Widely written-about topics, everyday language, popular code.

items.heading: Shaky on the rare
items.text: Niche facts, exact figures, small organisations, recent changes.

items.heading: No index to check
items.text: It can’t look up where it learned something, so it can’t easily tell what it doesn’t know.

quiz.question: During its first stage of training, how does a model mostly learn?
options: By predicting the next token across huge amounts of text and adjusting when it’s wrong
By having facts typed into a database by hand
quiz.explanation: The first stage is next-token prediction at enormous scale, with the parameters nudged after each mistake.

quiz.question: Why might a model straight out of the first stage not answer questions well?
options: It hasn’t read enough text yet
It was trained to continue text, not to follow instructions
quiz.explanation: Following instructions and acting as an assistant come from the second stage of training.

quiz.question: A big news story broke last week. Why might a model not know about it?
options: News is filtered out of all training
Its training text was collected before the story happened
Models can only learn about history
quiz.explanation: The model’s knowledge stops at its training cut-off. Only tools such as web search can add newer information to the context.
